utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we have asked the Prosecution to resume its examination-in-chief, I'd like to draw the attention of the parties to the fact that we are now starting at 12 minutes past 9.00. I take this opportunity because I myself was late, but not 12 minutes late. I had a good reason for it, and I take it that whenever someone is late, that there should be a good reason for that. Of course, it can happen. The Chamber is late now and then as well. But very often it happens that the Chamber is waiting outside, waiting either for resolution of technical problems or the arrival of whoever it is. So I'm in the happy position not to blame anyone for it, but I'd like at the same time to encourage everyone to be there at such time that we do not lose, as today, 12 minutes. And again, I'm to be blamed myself this morning, so therefore it's encouraging the Chamber as well not unnecessarily to cause a late start. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom, and at the same time Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic. Please be seated. Mr. Tomic, also good morning to you. Mr. Mandic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mentioned the other day when the Court inquired, I think actually counsel inquired about the date of a particular document, that it had been dated essentially by contextualisation. I have one document that may shed some light on the effort to identify the date of the document in -- through that manner, and so I'd ask to have that marked next in order. That's R0172473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, P458 is what appears to be a fax coming from UNPROFOR of eight pages. The date of the cover page is 27 July 1992 and it transmits messages to Mr. Colin Doyle from Ms. Sabina Berberovic, a message to Lord Carrington from Alija Izetbegovic and there is attached on the last two pages a list of prisons and detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, if I could just direct your attention to the last two pages of that document and simply ask you if the list reflected here appears to be the kind of list that was submitted in this case by the Bosnian side, listing places in which they claimed Muslims were being held by Serb authorities or Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document bearing the signature of Mr. Vukovic is a document of the State Commission for Exchange of War Prisoners of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was delivered to the international community, containing the places where there were prisoners held by the Serb side, that is, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe it was yesterday when we were listening to Ms. Biljana Plavsic that we discussed her denying certain allegations put forth by Mr. Vukovic concerning some places that are actually outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, like Serbia and Montenegro, like Nis, Belgrade, Herceg-Novi, Niksic, and so on and so forth. Mr. Prosecutor, I've already said that as Ms. Plavsic was responding to this, to a journalist, Gligorijevic, I believe, that both sides produced such lists for propaganda purposes. I'm not quite sure that they would have four to five places within each municipality where they would keep people, but I myself had never seen this particular list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I just seek some clarification? I think your testimony yesterday was that the statement of Mrs. Plavsic, that that was war propaganda, rather than the list. And I would like to invite you to perhaps look at this list and see how many locations exactly are outside the Serb-controlled territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so outside the state boundaries. You mentioned Belgrade. I see two entries Belgrade. I see one entry Nis. I see one entry Niksic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loznica. Your Honour, Loznica sports centre under item 22, Belgrade Batajnica, military airfield 28; Belgrade, the 4th of July barracks, 29; Nis military camp, 30; Subotica collection centre, 31; Herceg-Novi, under item 34 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Niksic, 35. I can't make out the two last ones because it's a poor copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we've got several on page 1 and then on page 2 I cannot find any, but perhaps my knowledge of the geography is not perfect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second page contains places that are all in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'd like to move on to Prosecution's next in order, which is an intercepted telephone conversation on April 20th, 1992, involving Mr. Cedo Kljajic, Mr. Tomislav Kovac, and then between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P459 and P459A for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there -- in respect of the previous exhibit, is there any translation into B/C/S? Because the list, of course, is not very much in need of any translation. But the letter, of course, you tendered that into evidence as well, and usually evidence should be in a language the accused understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. We'll have that translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Of course, let's be very practical. Unless the Defence would agree of only tendering the list. I mean, the question -- questions were only about the list, so of course the Defence could look at how important the letter is. You paid no attention to it at all. If that would help us out, then it would save us a lot of resources for translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the Defence is invited to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If it's acceptable to the Defence and we should give Mr. Stewart an opportunity to review it and consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think if I -- may I leave it this way, Your Honour, that Mr. Tieger has offered to have it translated. We accept the offer. But if perhaps in the course of this morning, if we notify them that we don't need a translation of that, then we'll work that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're invited to consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll mention for the benefit of the booth that this intercepted telephone conversation, as the others, it is in Sanction, and they should know that in order to play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any technical problem which prevents us from hearing the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apparently not, Your Honour. And I should mention for the Court's benefit, there are two clips to this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Cedo KLJAJIC: Hello. Tomislav KOVAC: Yes. Cedo KLJAJIC: Tomo. Tomislav KOVAC: Yes. Cedo KLJAJIC: It is Cedo Kljajic. How are you? Tomislav KOVAC: How are you, Cedo? Cedo KLJAJIC: What's up, buddy? Tomislav KOVAC: Well, fuck it ... Cedo KLJAJIC: What are you doing? Tomislav KOVAC: Well, fuck it, I'm clearing this shit up. Fuck it they make a mess and ... Cedo KLJAJIC: I know. Tomislav KOVAC: Yes. Cedo KLJAJIC: Well, Momo called Djeric up there some minutes ago. Tomislav KOVAC: Yes. Cedo KLJAJIC: To Pale. Well, regarding these checkpoints set up there. Tomislav KOVAC: Yes. Cedo KLJAJIC: Well, it is their and our unanimous opinion that those should not be impenetrable for all, you know, but that people should be allowed to pass, fuck it. Tomislav KOVAC: Listen, you do not know the decision of the Crisis Staff of Ilidza, that it made a decision to block life in Ilidza. Cedo KLJAJIC: Mico is up there at the moment. He went this evening, well, to Pale, and here Momo wants to talk to you. Tomislav KOVAC: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: Tomo. Tomislav KOVAC: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: How are you, head, head of the security service centre? Tomislav KOVAC: Well, fuck me ... Momcilo MANDIC: Come on, put that Prstojevic in prison, fuck him ... Tomislav KOVAC: Who? Momcilo MANDIC: That Prstojevic. Tomislav KOVAC: Come on, fuck it. In prison, don't fuck with me. Take politics into consideration. Momcilo MANDIC: I've just phoned Djeric and Krajisnik, man, and they say it has been ordered that checkpoints should be flexible. Tomislav KOVAC: And they have made the decision yesterday to block life in Ilidza, man, so that not a pedestrian ... Momcilo MANDIC: Who made the decision? Tomislav KOVAC: Well, the Ilidza Crisis Staff, man. Momcilo MANDIC: But, man, that is ... They have made a wrong decision. They cannot make such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can you first tell us who the participants in this conversation are.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Participants in this conversation are Cedo Kljajic, the under-secretary for public security, or chief of police at the level of Republika Srpska; Tomo Kovac, the then chief of the security centre of Ilidza; and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the conversation -- in the course of the conversation, Mr. Kovac and -- well, in the portion of the conversation we heard, Mr. Kljajic mentions Mico, and we can see from the transcript that that is in response to a question by Mr. Kovac: "Tell me, is Mico Stanisic there?" Can you identify for us with respect to those who participated in the conversation and Mico Stanisic the hierarchy of the Bosnian Serb MUP at that time with respect to those individuals, Mico Stanisic, yourself, Mr. Kljajic, and Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic was the MUP minister. I was deputy at the time on the 24th. I was Mico's deputy. Kljajic was the chief of the public security service, and Kovac was the chief of the security centre of Ilidza. This was the problem in the beginning of the war, when the crisis staffs wanted to take control over the municipalities, and they wanted to control the movement of civilians and people in general within their territories, which was not in accordance with the decisions of the political leadership, either the prime minister or Mr. Krajisnik. I proposed here that this particular president should be locked up, this president of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Ilidza, Prstojevic, who ordered the full blockade of movement in Ilidza. Kljajic could not do that, because the police could not lock up municipal functionaries. And I believe that this was a problem experienced in the beginning of the war, in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been drawn to mention that Mr. Tieger's last question identified a passage in the intercept which was in fact between the two clips that were actually played.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I attempted to mention that that was not a portion of the intercept that had been played, but instead it appeared in the transcript just before the second clip began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any confusion with the witness at this moment on this point? Or should it be read to him? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The predicate for the question, Your Honour, was that in the course of the portion of the intercept that was played, Mr. Kljajic mentioned Mico. I indicated that in the transcript of the intercept, that mention of Mico occurs in response to a question about Mico Stanisic, which can be seen on the transcript but not heard on the portion that was played.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, my observation is only really a minor one, which is that if there's -- if there's a purpose in playing these intercepts at all, rather simply showing the text to the witness, it's -- it's really a false saving to take out a tiny bit in the middle between two clips rather than play the whole thing through as the basis of the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a general rule you're right, but I think it's no reason to replay at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm not requesting that in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the point is valid, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Mandic, you became aware of this issue in Ilidza and contacted the political leadership and then advised Mr. Kovac in this conversation that Mr. Djeric and Mr. Krajisnik had ordered that the checkpoints should be flexible?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question misstates the -- I've just noticed as I'm looking at it. Misstates what's said in the transcript, because it's -- putting it to the witness in those terms and asking him to confirm is not the correct way of putting it because that's at -- then advise Mr. Kovac in this conversation that Mr. Djeric and Mr. Krajisnik had ordered that the checkpoints should be flexible. In fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll ask the question if Mr. Stewart is insisting on clarification. Again, these are matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you mind letting me finish, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Tieger offers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He doesn't know what I'm going to say, does he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first thing is that you say that the question misstates what's in the transcript and Mr. Tieger now offers to correct that in such a way. So let's first wait how Mr. Tieger proceeds and then if there's still any remaining issue, then we'll see that. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before this conversation took place, had you been advised of the problem in Ilidza concerning checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Cedo Kljajic who informed me of the problem, and he, in turn, was informed by Tomo Kovac according to the hierarchy in MUP. Then I called Mr. Djeric and consulted with Mr. Krajisnik as to what was supposed to be done with these decisions of the Crisis Staff that nearly blocked life in municipalities by blocking these checkpoints. The police asked for the situation to be kept under control in order to prevent violence from escalating, to have these checkpoints to control the movement of vehicles, weapons, ammunition, and so on. Because it was highly likely that there would be such flow of weapons. And this Prstojevic, who was the chief of the Crisis Staff, he seemed to have blocked life in Ilidza, according to what was said by Kljajic. And I said, well, I thought he was not really all there, and I thought that he had to be locked away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Krajisnik tell you in response to the information you provided about the problem?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I consulted him on this issue, Mr. Prosecutor. This was a long time ago. Rather, I consulted Mr. Djeric, but I also might have asked for Mr. Krajisnik's advice, because I did sometimes ask for his advice and he told me that life should not be blocked, that however, the police should continue keeping the situation under control and continue with the check-ups as was the case in Pale. But this was generally the problem in the beginning of the war. There was this conflict between the civilian and military authorities, the police, on the other hand, the infrastructures were severed, there was severed communication between the municipal, regional, and the republic levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The intercept from --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- after five minutes or so, or two, three minutes, whatever, we have not dealt with the point that I was going to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may raise the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was this, Your Honour, that at page 10, line 7, what Mr. Tieger put to the witness was: "Mr. Mandic, you became aware of this issue in Ilidza and contacted the political leadership and then advised Mr. Kovac in this conversation that Mr. Djeric and Mr. Krajisnik had ordered that the checkpoints should be flexible."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I am going to interrupt Mr. Stewart at this point. That was a question I was just about to ask. He has an uncanny ability to interrupt an examination just before the question is going to be asked by the Prosecution. So whether or not to formulate in his own way, I don't know, but I think it should have been clear as I directed the witness's attention to the intercept that that is precisely where I was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So uncanny is my instinct that it's a fantastic coincidence, but I will just sit down and see where we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both counsel are invited to allow each other to perform their tasks in a smooth way, not to intervene unnecessarily, and not to add to a slight irritation that seems to exist. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the intercept transcript indicates -- well, in the course of the conversation, you state: "I've just phoned Djeric and Krajisnik, man, and they say it has been ordered that checkpoints should be flexible." First of all, I take it you confirm that in 1992, speaking to Mr. Kovac just after the -- just as the event was happening and just after you had been in contact with the leadership in Pale, you indicated to Mr. Kovac that you had just phoned Djeric and Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you said: "I've just phoned Djeric and Krajisnik, man, and they say it has been ordered that checkpoints should be flexible." Who ordered that checkpoints should be flexible?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political leadership of Republika Srpska. I was probably told both by Mr. Djeric and Mr. Krajisnik about that. However, who took the decision personally, I don't know, but I did call only these two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to next move to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that is the extent to which my point which I've twice tried to make but not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Make your point. If there's any remaining point, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. It's this, that at page 10, line 7, the passage - I'll have to start it again cause it's four or five lines - the question was: "And Mr. Mandic, you became aware of this issue in Ilidza and contacted the political leadership and then advised Mr. Kovac in this conversation that Mr. Djeric and Mr. Krajisnik had ordered that the checkpoints should be flexible." In fact, the intercept does not say that. It says: "I've just phoned --" this is just below the middle of the second page of the English, Mr. Mandic: "I've just phoned Djeric and Krajisnik man and they say it has been ordered that checkpoints should be flexible." Which is different. It's plainly different. And the witness said "yes." My concern is this: That Mr. Tieger has asked further questions and it eventually got to a question which specifically asked about who had ordered. But if we have on the record a question and answer like that, yes, this indicates the -- the dangers of putting to a witness a question which is potentially confusingly close to what was actually said in the intercept, but is in fact inaccurate. So my submission is that questions in that form should be corrected in the sense that they should then be withdrawn, because it isn't fair that a question and answer like that remains on the record when the question contained has such a clear error in the representation of the text of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, first of all, in the further questions it has been become abundantly clear that the way Mr. Tieger presented the text of the intercept was not fully correct and that finally the specific question was put to the witness and he gave a clear answer that it was not -- at least that he has no knowledge on Mr. Djeric and Mr. Krajisnik ordering anything about flexibility of checkpoints. So that has been clarified sufficiently and the transcript will be read not letter by letter but in -- as a whole. Next time, if a similar thing happens, I think one line would do. If you would just have asked me or invited Mr. Tieger to quote the part of the transcript literally, that would have taken just seven seconds and that would certainly have been followed by Mr. Tieger, and if not, I would have instructed him to do so. And then I think we would have come to a point where both the Defence, you, and I said that both parties should allow each other to perform their tasks, that you would have done your task and that, at the same time, the examination of the witness would have been more smooth. So, therefore, that's to say -- just some guidance on how to do that next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, I submit that's a most unfair --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And any reading of the transcript will indicate if I had been allowed courteously to make my objection in very short terms, this matter would have been dealt with about five minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'd like to turn next to another intercepted telephone conversation during that same general period of time. That's a conversation that has already been marked and the first portion of which we began to play at the end of one session. It's 429, I believe. And that's a conversation between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Kovac. We never actually played it. We just had it marked and then we began to play it and only got through the first couple of sentences, I think, before encountering some technical difficulties. So we should play it. Again, it's on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Momcilo MANDIC: What was that telephone number in Ilidza again? Tomislav KOVAC: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Momo Mandic on the phone. Who is there? Tomislav KOVAC: Momo, Tomo here. Momcilo MANDIC: Tomo, how are you? Tomislav KOVAC: Well. Momcilo MANDIC: Tell me, what's up in Ilidza? Tomislav KOVAC: Fuck, a lot. Momcilo MANDIC: Are there big problems? Tomislav KOVAC: Well, we are holding our territory, you know. Momcilo MANDIC: Is it now getting critical or what? Momcilo MANDIC: And do you have any heavy weaponry? Tomislav KOVAC: Okay. We have heavy weaponry on the side, on the side. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes. And give a warning. Alert stage one. Tomo, please tell me I am in Vraca. I came to Vraca and if, call for God's sake, and us ten or what will come. I don't know these territorial defenders from Novo Sarajevo motherfuckers. I don't even know who is in charge of them nor what they are not [as interpreted]. One have to inform Vojkovici and Lukavica in time to shell Sokolovic Kolonija in case they attack you. Tomislav KOVAC: Listen, if this happens, Momo, we have to get this straight. We can't take this any more. We can't just be defending here around Ilidza, you understand. We have to organise ourselves and either win this thing or lose. We can't take this any more. They attack. We stop them. They attack again. If there is a chance we should finish them off once for all I suggest that we attack Sokolovic Kolonija from both sides. Momcilo MANDIC: As for me, it should be destroyed. I would level it to the ground. Tomislav KOVAC: They provoked everything. I feel sorry for those moderate Muslims who don't want that. Momcilo MANDIC: We need to. These people are from Sandzak. I would them -- Tomislav KOVAC: People from Sandzak they trick them and people die in Butmir Hrasnica, motherfuckers. Why don't they stop them? Momcilo MANDIC: You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do have a feeling that some of the transcript was missing, although it was very difficult to hear the tape. But it does seem that we had fewer text than was actually uttered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this observation. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears that the last page of the English translation was not provided to the interpreters, and perhaps I can direct the witness's attention to that and make sure it's read and translated. It's just a few lines, as the Court may be able to see from its own transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wouldn't it be wise to have that last part read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That seems not necessarily to be the same point that the interpreters are making. The comments seem to refer to bits where they did in fact have the transcript but that they suggested that there was less text in those passages than what was actually said, which seems to be a slightly different point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be of any use to replay it and to see whether in a second round we could come to a more perfect presentation of the -- of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The difficulty is that the spoken language runs so fast that it is difficult to actually even follow by sight, the text, and the quality is very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we could inquire whether or not the booth has the -- has three pages of an English translation, which of course -- which I suspect is the source of the problem, but may not be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first check whether you have all of the English translation. Do you have three pages, last page containing only some 10 or 11 lines?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have what seems to be written here as 3 of 6 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Last page starting with "Kovac Tomislav: I have all extremists in Ilidza" ... ? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the problem remains, Mr. Tieger, that the interpreters cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar draws my attention to the fact that also there was a hold, they stopped in the middle and they restarted again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two clips to this intercept. Otherwise we'll be playing more than is necessary, it seems to me, and I would also -- I'll be directing questions to the second clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If that's of any assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where does the second clip then start.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It should begin with Mr. Kovac -- it begins in the middle of the English translation, second page, with Mr. Kovac saying: "We are controlling Ilizda."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ilidza. Then let's perhaps replay that part and see whether -- if one of the interpreters could try to follow the audio and see whether it's reflected well in the B/C/S version and if the other interpreter would then perhaps read those parts and report to me at the very end whether it was still too speedy to follow. Could we replay the second clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Tomislav KOVAC: We are controlling Ilidza but we received information from three sides that Juka Prazina already has mounted mortars with the intention of shelling us. Momcilo MANDIC: From where? Tomislav KOVAC: Otes. Momcilo MANDIC: From Otes or what? Momcilo MANDIC: And do you have any heavy weaponry? Tomislav KOVAC: Okay. We have heavy weaponry on the side ... on the side ... Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, yes, and give a warning. Alert stage one, Tomo. Please tell me. I am in these Territorial Defence [as interpreted], I came to Vraca. I'm in Vraca. I came to Vraca and if, call for God's sake, and us ten or what will come. I don't know these territorial defenders from Novo Sarajevo motherfuckers. I don't even know who is in charge of them nor what they are at. We have to inform Vojkovici and Lukavica in time to shell Sokolovic Kolonija in case they attack you. Tomislav KOVAC: Listen, if this happens, Momo, we have to get this straight. We can't take this any more. We can't just be defending here around Ilidza, you understand, we have to organise ourselves once and either win this thing other lose. We can't take this any more. They attack. We stop them. They attack again. If there is a chance we should finish them off once for all. I suggest that we attack Sokolovic Kolonija for both side. Momcilo MANDIC: As for me it should be destroyed. I would level it to the ground. Tomislav KOVAC: They provoked everything. I feel sorry for those moderate Muslims who don't want that. Momcilo MANDIC: We need to. These people are from Sandzak. I would them ... Tomislav KOVAC: People from Sandzak, they trick them, and people die in Butmir and Hrasnica, motherfuckers, why don't they stop them. Momcilo MANDIC: You are absolutely right. Tomislav KOVAC: I have all extremists in Ilidza under my control and there is nothing else. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, Tomo, please tell me if anything happens, and prepare heavy artillery. And if anything moves engage immediately. I will level Sokolovic Kolonija to the ground, fuck them. I am going now to Lukavica to instruct those who have them in close tabs to level them if anything moves on Ilidza. Tomislav KOVAC: Okay. Momcilo MANDIC: We'll hear from each other. Tomislav KOVAC: Okay. Momcilo MANDIC: Bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- before I ask the interpreters, Mr. Tieger, are you going to put questions to the witness in relation to what he said or to what Mr. Kovac said? Because I tried to follow at least the -- I can't understand it, the words spoken by the two participants in this conversation, and I noticed that at least the text spoken by Mr. Mandic seems to be far more clear. Is that -- could you tell us whether the questions will be about the Kovac part or the Mandic part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Primarily directed to Mr. Mandic's comments, Your Honour, I think, but -- well, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we move into that area, you'll certainly be aware of it and I'll be -- I'll bear in mind the Court's observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the interpreters now whether it was possible to check whether the B/C/S spoken words appear more or less -- no, of course it should be precise on the transcript. Although I noticed that sometime there was a very short "yes" or just a short intervention by the other part, not really spoken words, which are missing in the transcript. Could you inform us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. The substantial part is there. There may be some expletives missing, but substantially it is all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honour, we're happy with the B/C/S transcript, Ms. Cmeric tells me that there really is no significant problem at all with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this conversation took place on April 23rd, 1992. That was the time when you were still deputy minister of the Bosnian Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in the latter part of the intercept, you say to Mr. Kovac: "Yes, Tomo. Please tell me if anything happens and prepare heavy artillery, and if anything moves, engage immediately." What -- when you told Mr. Kovac to engage immediately if anything moved, what did that refer to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momo Kovac held the municipality of Ilidza and even before the war he was the chief of MUP of Ilidza. The municipality was composed of several neighbourhoods, and between Hrasnica and Ilidza, there was the place called Sokolovic Kolonija, where Muslims from foreign countries came and settled there, and they launched several attacks and provoked war conflict and moved towards the centre of Ilidza. The other day when I broke into tears when my mother lived in Hrasnica, together with 95 per cent of Muslims, he had been living there for 40 years, and they took her to this centre in Sokolovic Kolonija and forced her several times to talk to me, to criticise me, and tell me not to do what I was doing. They manipulated a 70-year-old lady and then they returned her back to Hrasnica, where there was a majority Muslim population. This was done by the people who held Sokolovic Kolonija. We call them Sandzaklije. They came from abroad. They were extremists. Unlike those who we referred to as local Muslims and with whom we had been coexisting well. Being irritated with this and with these constant attacks, I told Tomo to do everything possible to prevent these people from coming to Ilidza and taking control of it. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that same passage of the intercept, you tell Mr. Kovac that you were now going to Lukavica to instruct those who have them in close tabs, to level them if anything moves in Ilidza. Who were those who -- in Lukavica who had them in close tabs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned here that that was the Territorial Defence or the reserve military troops, in other words, those people were recruited for the Army of Republika Srpska. There was a barracks in Lukavica called Slavisa Vajner Cica, which was the headquarters of the Sarajevo Corps of the former Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall if indeed you proceeded to Lukavica and instructed those in Lukavica with respect to Sokolovic Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that I went there to give instructions to the army how to wage a war. I simply supported Tomo Kovac and I knew that these telephone conversations were listened in, and in order to prevent an attack on Ilidza by these extremists, as we saw them, and the Muslims from abroad who attacked Tomo Kovac on a daily basis, and he was so irritated that at one point he says: "Let this finish once and for all, and you can see that the leader of the Patriotic League, Juka Prazina - which was a paramilitary formation - was spotted near Ilidza. He was leading these extremist Muslims who had come from other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, we've been having really animated discussion here because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We tried to work out what's happening. It is sometimes extremely difficult for us to deal with this because there are flaws apparently in the English translation of this, and the problem we have is that that was in a question that Mr. Tieger asked at page 23, line 20. And I should say straight away that my -- the objection I made to an earlier question doesn't apply here, because Mr. Tieger's question was correctly, as far as it goes, based on the English text which he has in front of him and which I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You want to draw our attention to the flaws in the translation. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It isn't absolutely straightforward, Your Honour, because what is on the last page, it's -- Mr. Mandic saying, an answer -- or a part of the conversation, it says: "Yes, Tomo. Please tell me if anything happens. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps have this read by Ms. Cmeric and see whether an oral translation at this moment results in anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's a helpful suggestion, I think, Your Honour, because it is quite complicated, potentially, the translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Cmeric is invited to read the relevant part, and that would be the fifth box from the bottom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask the special attention of the interpreters for the translation of this part of the transcript. Please proceed, Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [As read] [Interpretation] "Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Tomo, please let me know if anything, and prepare this heavy artillery and that to engage if there were any movements. This Sokolovic Kolonija should be razed to the ground. Fuck their mother. Now I'll go now to Lukavica to those people that they are keeping them in cross-hairs to level if there was any movement in Ilidza."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The translation is slightly different from what we see on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour will see, and everybody's obviously doing their best, Your Honour will see that that can't have been a particularly easy sentence to translate, to interpret, the way it's ended up. But the key point, as Your Honour indicates, is the verb in the middle that's on the part of the verb that's missing. Well, it's not missing. It's just not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are some differences. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed, but I'd rather take the, well, new translation as the valid one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I assumed that was the case, Your Honour. Thank you. And I'll inquire accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I think you indicated in the course of your responses that Mr. Kovac was concerned and upset when he spoke with you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you again: Did you go to Lukavica in response to the information he provided or the concerns he expressed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Mr. Prosecutor. I just said, Momo, as a matter of preventive measure, if you come again under the attack from Juka Prazina and I would try these people from Lukavica to defend Ilidza from these extremists. This was a kind of pre-emptive action on my side, because Tomo expressed concern that he would not be able to maintain Ilidza in the condition that he had taken it originally in. I informed him that I had ten men in the school in Vrace, and I went there on the 6th of April and stayed there for about one month. That's a part situated between Grbavica and Lukavica neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that you indicated in the earlier part of your comment to Mr. Kovac at the end of this conversation that you wanted to be informed if anything happened, and also instructed him with respect to heavy artillery. But both translations of the intercept indicate that you said to Mr. Kovac that you will go now to Lukavica. So are you suggesting that simply telling him that you would go to Lukavica, whether or not you went, was in some way of assistance to him? In what way was simply telling him that you were going to Lukavica be a preventive measure rather than actually going and conveying the situation as he had related it to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall going to Lukavica, but I did try to raise his spirits, that he was not going to be abandoned if he comes under attack from two or three sides, that I was going to assist him from Vojkovici, Lukavica, wherever there were Serb forces, be it military, police, or Crisis Staff forces. I tried to encourage him this way, because he said he was unable to hold on on his own, that he had to defend Ilidza from different sides, and that the major danger was posed by these extremists from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina that were at Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, did the Bosnian Serbs also -- you've indicated now that there were Muslims from outside Sarajevo who came into Sarajevo to assist in the war effort against Serbs. Did the Bosnian Serbs have the assistance of Serbs from outside Sarajevo, Serb radicals or Serb extremists from outside Sarajevo, who came in to assist the Serbs against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the war, there were Serbs coming from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina to fight the war on the side with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that include the paramilitary forces of Arkan or Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and many others. There were several of these paramilitary units, mostly from Serbia, though some were from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For example, do you know who Legija was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the war, I didn't know who Legija was. That was not his name during the war. It was later on in Belgrade that I found out who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And regardless of the name he went by at the time, did you know with which forces he was associated or involved with?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you find out later with which forces he was engaged?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legija was one of the commanders of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's Panthers. Later on, I found out that he was one of his commanders, one of his main people. That was later on, when I came to live in Belgrade, in 1993, that is, in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was Legija and the forces under his control operating in Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I found this out from a document that you showed to me in October, or was it in March last year? Legija used to be called "Cema." His family name was Ulemek. The man seemed to change names quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know about -- you mentioned that, in a response to an earlier question, that you also knew about Seselj's forces operating in Sarajevo in -- let me ask you: Was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was 1992 or 1993, it was in the beginning of the war that certain units arrived who presented themselves as radicals. Among them was one man by the name of Aleksic, first name Slavko. He held the positions at the Jewish cemetery in Sarajevo. This man was from Bileca, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, but who used to live and work in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did Seselj's forces and any other forces coming in from outside Sarajevo to assist the Bosnian Serbs in their efforts against Muslims work with and coordinate with local Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that with precision, but I do think that some units placed themselves under the command of the army and some under the command of the police. Whether some of them operated independently through municipal crisis staffs, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could have you listen to an intercepted telephone conversation from around that time and it might shed some additional light on this very area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would be a telephone conversation of April 23rd, 1992 between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Kovac, marked ET 0322-0086. I'm sorry. My apologies. That is still looking at the old exhibit. I'm referring now and what should be marked next in order is a conversation of 21 April 1992 between Mr. Mandic and a gentleman named Igor. That is marked ET 0324-9691.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P460 and P460A for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, this is in the Sanction presentation mode, for the benefit of the booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Momcilo MANDIC: This is Momo. Who's calling? Igor: Igor. Momcilo MANDIC: Igor, what's up? Igor: Fucked up. They are shelling us. Fuck it. Momcilo MANDIC: Who is shelling you? Igor: Fuck it. A mortar hit Pavilion 10 and then snipers ... Fuck it. Momcilo MANDIC: Tell me, there are some of Seselj's guys encircled down at Palma. Can somebody help them? Send down some of our Territorial Defence guys. Tell it there, pass a message to pull the people out of there. Fuck it. Seselj has just called now from Belgrade. Igor: Aha. Since then, isn't it? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Igor: I don't know, but I'll see to it with Karisik now. Momcilo MANDIC: Tell Karo, is Mico down there? Igor: No. Which Mico? Stanisic? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Igor: No, there is nobody. Momcilo MANDIC: How come? Igor: They are in the field. What do I know? Momcilo MANDIC: Out there, are they? Igor: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: Please, let them know, to make them stronger, if nothing else. How far did our guys come? Igor: They are retreating. Momcilo MANDIC: They are retreating, are they? Igor: That's the information I have, I'm telling you again. Momcilo MANDIC: How far have they retreated? Igor: What the fuck do I know? I don't know. Momcilo MANDIC: Please, pass the message. Igor: I'll see to it with Karisik. Momcilo MANDIC: Just to pull out the people ... Igor: Yes, yes, yes. Brno has also been wounded. Momcilo MANDIC: Brno, has he? Igor: As soon as he set forth, the bullet got him, you know? Momcilo MANDIC: Aha. Igor: There are no more than ten or eleven of them. Momcilo MANDIC: What? Igor: There are ten or eleven of them, not more. Momcilo MANDIC: Good, five to ten people. Igor: Fine, I'll see to it with Karisik. I'll tell me him that. Momcilo MANDIC: Please, let it be seen. Don't, then, there. Only these -- let Karisik be ready and let here -- fuck their mothers in the mouth. Can't he raise the Elektroprivreda building to the ground with those three-barrelled mortars from there. Igor: They are shelling non-stop. Fuck it. But they have lots of checkpoints. There is a Secondary Commercial School, Elektroprivreda, Social Welfare, I don't know. They also seized the Secondary Commercial School there, fuck it. Momcilo MANDIC: Who? Igor: The Green Berets. Momcilo MANDIC: The Secondary Commercial School, did they? Igor: Yes. Fuck it. Momcilo MANDIC: Who planned it like that. Is he -- is here ... Igor: They started it hastily, without a good assessment, without anything. They were counting on around 300 people and 50 responded, there. Momcilo MANDIC: Son of a bitch. Tell me, Zlatiste, what's going on with it? Has it been touched at all? Igor: It hasn't been. Fuck. I said it there last night when we talked like people, first you liberate Zlatiste, you have both for assistance and for ... and for ... retreat, damn you. They are thinking of take the hospital. All big ... son of a bitch. Momcilo MANDIC: Right, please give a message to ... if it is possible to finish that. Igor: I'll see to it now ... Momcilo MANDIC: That they don't stay in the encirclement. Igor: Good. Momcilo MANDIC: At Palma. Igor: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can you first tell us who Igor was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he is. There was one Igor Velasevic who was with me at SUP Vrace. He was a member of SUP of Republika Srpska, if this is indeed Igor Velasevic. But I do believe so. I'm not sure, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You tell Igor in the early part of the conversation that -- to "Send some of our Territorial Defence guys, tell it there -- pass a message to pull the people out of there. Fuck it. Seselj has just called now from Belgrade." And was Seselj's call from Belgrade specifically referring to his men in Sarajevo and their situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what it's all about, Mr. Prosecutor. Pavilion 10 was under attack here. This was within the compound of the school for the interior where the MUP and the special MUP forces were stationed. When we advanced towards Vrace, that was on the 4th of April. On the right-hand side, there's this Pavilion 10, which Igor mentions as having been attacked. Seselj phoned some of the functionaries at Pale who informed us, in turn, whether it was Mico Stanisic or some of the leading persons in MUP, that a group of radicals from Sarajevo, these were Seselj's radicals, who appeared -- who were ambushed at Palma pastry shop. I was there with Karisik, who was a commander of a special MUP unit, and I was discussing with him to try and deliver people from the encirclement there. This is maybe -- this was one kilometre away as the crow flies. That is the distance between the seat of the Serb MUP and this Palma establishment. This area was encircled by an active unit belonging to the Muslims, who wanted to drive or destroy the units encircled there at Vrace. Brno is one of these -- Seselj's radicals, Vojvodas, who lived in Sarajevo. He was born either at Sokolac or at Pale, if that is the man. I even know his family name. Gavrilovic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this would be an appropriate time to break, unless the Court has some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no questions at this moment. But I would like first to ask Madam Usher to escort Mr. Mandic and Mr. Tomic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I carefully analysed what happened and what caused the irritation. Mr. Stewart, you took 26 seconds to explain to us that Mr. Tieger was misstating the transcript, which he did; that -- you looked that up. I would not expect anyone to say such a thing if he would not have looked that up. That putting it wrongly and asking confirmation to a witness is not the correct way of doing. That needs no explanation at all, because that's a common understanding. Then after 26 seconds, Mr. Tieger, who seemed to have become impatient, which he preferably not should become, responded and said that he would put the question, and then you responded, Mr. Stewart, by saying that Mr. Tieger did not even know what you were about to say. And then Mr. Tieger put a new question and then I don't know whether that was all lost time or whether that were questions that would have been put anyhow. Misstating a transcript of -- or an earlier testimony of a witness is wrong. That needs no explanation whatsoever, and should be corrected as soon as possible. Mr. Tieger, if Mr. Stewart takes 26 seconds and has not yet explained what he wants to say, apart from these generalities which are common understanding, then becoming impatient usually does not serve a smooth continuation of the questioning of the witness. Therefore, what should have been done is that Mr. Stewart would, and that would have taken him four or five seconds, to ask whether or not through me, to invite Mr. Tieger to correctly state the transcript, to correctly present the transcript. He then would have done so, I take it, and then questions would have been asked. Mr. Tieger, when Mr. Stewart took quite some time to explain to us exactly what he wanted, sometimes it's better to give him five more seconds, and that would have resolved the matter. Then finally, Mr. Stewart, at the very end after the five minutes -- I'm not blaming you for taking the time to -- saying that it was totally unfair of me, but at least you took one and a half more minutes to explain to us that it was misstating and that is incorrect, et cetera. Therefore, this is my analysis of the situation. I think I gave the parties guidance as to how to behave under those circumstances. As a general rule, if, in a question, there's any misstatement of either testimony or statement or transcript of an intercept, you're invited to ask for a literal quote, and asking for a literal quote means that you're not satisfied with the way the transcript or the statement or the intercept is presented by the other party. That's my guidance. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you escort the witness and Mr. Tomic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'd like to move next to an intercepted telephone conversation of July 10th, 1992, between Mr. Mandic and Ivo Rezo, and then Mr. Mandic and Branko Kvesic. That is marked ET 0328-2468, and it consists of five clips in the Sanction mode.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P461 and P461A for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This doesn't seem to be the beginning of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution indicate where the interpreters have to look in order to translate the portion played.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first clip begins at the bottom of page 3 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have the interpreters found that? Then could we replay the relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You'll find it beginning at line 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not hear any translation. Apart from that, Mr. Tieger, line 43 in the English is a bit problematic, because the line numbering goes until 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, the problem may have been that when we restarted this clip it began in the middle of the clip rather than at the beginning, and would have made it difficult for the translators to follow if they were directed to the bottom of page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine. So could we start -- could you tell us exactly -- we now start at the bottom of page 3, line 34 or --?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 43 on the line transcript. In any event, the line that begins: "There's no sense to wage a war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The sixth line up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it possible that Mr. Tieger has got different line numbering from the rest of the world?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Must be. Mr. Tieger, our line numbering goes until 34 on each page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's quite right. There are -- it's been formatted in two different ways. Looking at page 7, line 25 for the beginning of this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That makes now sense. Have the interpreters found the relevant portion? Yes. Then could we restart, then, the intercept to be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Now the transcript is starting from the beginning. Ivo REZO: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Ivo REZO: Are you doing, gorgeous? I just wanted to call you. Ivo REZO: Huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before we reach page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will be a long time before we get to page 7. That's quite right. Momcilo MANDIC: There is no sense to wage a war now, you know. Branko KVESIC: No fucking way. Momcilo MANDIC: Counts and national communities have already taken everything that was supposed to be taken. I don't know. Sarajevo is disputable. The area down there in Herzegovina and up there along the Sava River. There is nothing else left. Branko KVESIC: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: I think that we should not wage a war because of it any more. Branko KVESIC: We should fucking finish this as soon as possible. Momcilo MANDIC: Our people are for it. Branko KVESIC: Are they? Momcilo MANDIC: I just don't know what to do with the Turks, fuck it. Pay them 24 salaries and let them go, brother. There should be an airlift established with Turkey and let them go and we should split Bosnia in two parts. Branko KVESIC: I told them that the only normal thing for them would be to have a status of a nation if they accept to have counties. Do you understand? Serbs Croats and Muslims could live in a single state of Bosnia and Herzegovina divided in counties. It shouldn't be divided but organised according to counties. Momcilo MANDIC: Wait a minute. But they are a minority now, man. Branko KVESIC: What? Momcilo MANDIC: They are a minority now. Fuck. Branko KVESIC: There is no way to build a unitary country, either Serbian or Croatian any more. Momcilo MANDIC: They are the smallest nation in number now. Branko KVESIC: Yes. Either Muslim -- what parts of the town are you controlling? Momcilo MANDIC: It is mostly the left bank of the Miljacka River. We don't control Alpasino, a part of Mojmilo, and Otoka only. Everything else on this side from the Vrbanja bridge onwards is ours. Branko KVESIC: Really? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Branko KVESIC: And the area up there to Elektroprivreda; right? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Branko KVESIC: Are you still there? Momcilo MANDIC: Including Hrasno and Pere Kosorica Square down there and everything else. Branko KVESIC: Really? Momcilo MANDIC: Up to the barracks Viktor Bubanj. Then they control the area down there. Branko KVESIC: Yes. I've noticed that Croats are leaving. They have some kind of HVO, right? Momcilo MANDIC: People say that many Croats have left. Branko KVESIC: Yes. They let them go. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Branko KVESIC: All right. That's the right way to do. They shouldn't create problems. Momcilo MANDIC: Everything joins his people, his own people. Branko KVESIC: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the benefit of the Court, counsel, and the booth, clip 2 begins at page 10, approximately line 12 or 13. Branko KVESIC: Well, I said to this man here ... someone has hung up the phone right now. Momcilo MANDIC: Munja. Branko KVESIC: Who is recording this? You or ...? Momcilo MANDIC: Munja. Fuck. He broadcasts everything that I talk about on television and radio. Did you know it? Branko KVESIC: Are you serious? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Branko KVESIC: You are kidding me. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, he is really quick-witted. Branko KVESIC: I can see how smart you are. You wrote it in Latin script on one side and on the other side you wrote it in Cyrillic script. Momcilo MANDIC: We don't want to have a single nation state, man. We want to have a democratic state where the Serbian people would be in the majority. Branko KVESIC: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: So Croats and Muslims would also have rights. Excuse me, Croats and the rest of Muslims ... after we clean them out. Branko KVESIC: All right. Tell me, what ... those prisoners. Momcilo MANDIC: We set them all free, man. As far as the HVO is concerned, we do not have any prisoners. Branko KVESIC: But, they have. Momcilo MANDIC: We have none here. It was agreed on a higher level that no man of Croatian ethnicity should be detained. Branko KVESIC: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: There is no one here. They all go over there, towards Kiseljak immediately. Branko KVESIC: All right. As for that area over there, it is so. But tell me, what can you do over there ... There is a friend of yours who told me about one of your ... What was his name? Hang on a minute. It was some person, Madzarevic. Momcilo MANDIC: Where is he from? Branko KVESIC: Well, did you put in a request for him? Momcilo MANDIC: It was probably some kind of intervention. It was probably some intervention by my ... Branko KVESIC: There are some of our men in Manjaca, man. Momcilo MANDIC: In Krajina; right? Branko KVESIC: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: We can do it. Branko KVESIC: What can you do about it. Momcilo MANDIC: A lot. Branko KVESIC: Listen, fuck, let's find out ... Listen, it is because of relations in general. Momcilo MANDIC: Naturally, man. Branko KVESIC: There is ... Momcilo MANDIC: All right. I'll tell it to my main boss. Branko KVESIC: Check it, please. Momcilo MANDIC: Where are they placed? Branko KVESIC: You know where I am? Momcilo MANDIC: I know it, but where are they placed over there? Branko KVESIC: They are placed somewhere on Manjaca. Momcilo MANDIC: Over there in the military camp on Manjaca? Branko KVESIC: Yes. There is Tole, Zrno, and the team of men who were in Zarkovo with Tole and who were betrayed by Muslims. Momcilo MANDIC: Aha. Branko KVESIC: The TO betrayed them when those Chetniks picked them up. Momcilo MANDIC: I will tell him that today if he returns from London. He should call and get it done because he's very much in the mood for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Clip 3 will begin at page 14, line 15 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Momcilo MANDIC: We are fighting for our people and our political rights. Branko KVESIC: Certainly. Momcilo MANDIC: And for the right to self-determination. Branko KVESIC: That's right. I always say that we should talk in this way with everyone who can help terminate this conflict instead of waging a war, to hell with it. Momcilo MANDIC: Naturally, man. Do you know that 100.000 people surely died in BH. Branko KVESIC: Seriously? Momcilo MANDIC: Well, yes, for sure. Branko KVESIC: Fuck. Momcilo MANDIC: They are hiding it over there, in Sarajevo, but they have terrible losses. Branko KVESIC: How many men have they lost in Sarajevo? Momcilo MANDIC: Many, tens of thousands. Branko KVESIC: You cannot be serious? Momcilo MANDIC: They have many casualties. I swear to my life. You know, they take them to a mosque and tell them: "You are martyrs now. If you get killed, you will cross to the other world ... equally." It is stupid. Branko KVESIC: Who is there in the former ministry now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Clip 4 at page 15, line 31

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Momcilo MANDIC: Vito is ... I think that they offered him ... Alija appointed him as assistant secretary in the department of trade. Branko KVESIC: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: Can you imagine ... While they were losing and now ... trade [sic]. Branko KVESIC: What? So, nothing. It means that he ... Nothing. His wife lost the job and he lost the apartment over there. Branko KVESIC: Really? Momcilo MANDIC: Muslims expelled him from Stari Grad. Branko KVESIC: What happened to him? He's a fool when ... Momcilo MANDIC: You know, I told you then. You could figure out everything then. He is really crazy. Well, Alija tricked him. A fool. Branko KVESIC: Well, yes, you are right. Momcilo MANDIC: He tricked him, a fool. He clung on to him for a few tens of thousands of German marks. Branko KVESIC: Well, yes. What can I tell you? When I take everything into consideration, as you said, the problem was in him. Momcilo MANDIC: In him only. Branko KVESIC: You know, he was behaving so in order not to run afoul of you or them, but one cannot ... Who can do it like that? Momcilo MANDIC: Believe me, everyone who has the same last name as he has in his birthplace, Sekovici, has no chance to survive. Do you believe it. Branko KVESIC: Seriously. Momcilo MANDIC: I swear to my mother. People see it as betrayal. Listen, you are to stick to your people. If they are mistaken, the entire nation is mistaken. Branko KVESIC: Well, yes, fuck, certainly, certainly. Momcilo MANDIC: You always used to tell him: "I am Ustasha, if so required. I follow my people. My people elected me. Fuck you." Branko KVESIC: That's right. Naturally. Momcilo MANDIC: And you were always right about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the fifth clip will begin at page 21, approximately line 12.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Momcilo MANDIC: Come home, please. I am really for it. Our men and children are getting killed for nothing and all ... I will talk with the boss as soon as he returns from London and ask him to meet your boss. Branko KVESIC: Yes. Momcilo MANDIC: I have this telephone number. I will call you and you will be in touch with our friend. We will arrange a meeting for them somewhere in our territories, have them sit together and get it finished, damn it. It concerns these two nations. As soon as they make an agreement, the third nation will also have to ... You know. Branko KVESIC: Then there should be contacts established on levels of police forces and many other organs. Momcilo MANDIC: The police and the army, and cooperation ... Without borders ... Branko KVESIC: There are many things. We cannot live like this, man. We won't be at war for a hundred fucking years. Momcilo MANDIC: I was for such solution from the very beginning, believe me. I was not for a unitary country, but I am for cooperation and for that ... Branko KVESIC: Listen, probably ... Please, check that thing for me over there on Manjaca. Momcilo MANDIC: I'll do it right away. Branko KVESIC: Tole and ... Momcilo MANDIC: I'll do it on Monday or Tuesday. I cannot do it any earlier. Branko KVESIC: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they cannot say when the tape was stopped and where the transcript was actually -- until what point should it be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you quite the interpreters what -- where the portion ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe the clip ended at the top of page 22, at approximately line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I'll do it right away"? That's -- no, I'm looking at the right page. Have the interpreters read the -- let me just see. Yes. As a matter of fact, you read a few lines more, I think one -- two times Kvesic and one time Mandic are too much in the transcript. So it stops at page 45, line 21: "I'll do it right away." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can we begin by having you simply identify the persons to whom you're speaking in the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic, formerly the under-secretary State Security joint MUP Bosnia-Herzegovina; Ivo Rezo former chief of the crime department of the Sarajevo SUP; and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how long had you known Mr. Rezo and Mr. Kvesic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known Ivo Rezo since we were 15, 16 years of age. I attended the police academy together with him. And I got to know Kvesic when he became under-secretary for state security and I became inspector for the crime department in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was their nationality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats, Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And where were they at the time you were having the conversation on April -- on July 10th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were on the premises of the district court in Sarajevo, in the Butmir neighbourhood at Kula. I believe so. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to a part of the conversation that was played in the first clip portion we heard, and that's toward the bottom of page 7 of the English translation, where you say: "There's no sense to wage a war now, you know." Kvesic says: "No fucking way," and you say, "Counties and national communities have already taken everything that was supposed to be taken. I don't know. Sarajevo is disputable, the area down there and Herzegovina and up there along the Sava River. There's nothing else left." Was that your assessment of status of the conflict at that point, in early July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was merely conveying the position of the state leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, when you say you were conveying the position of the state leadership of Republika Srpska, who in particular are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the state, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that Mr. Karadzic's sole view of the status of events at that point or did other members of the state leadership feel the same way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the others shared the same view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there any member of the leadership, as you have previously identified them, who felt otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you continue at that part of your conversation with Mr. Kvesic by -- well, he states to you: "We should fucking finish this as soon as possible." You say: "Our people are for it." Again, are you referring -- when you say "Our people are for it," are you referring to the state leadership, are you referring to the people generally? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then Kvesic says: "Are they?" And you say: "I just don't know what to do with the Turks. Fuck it. Pay them 24 salaries and let them go, brother. There should be an airlift established with Turkey and let them go. And we should split Bosnia in two parts."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like to hear my comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you a couple of questions first and then I'll certainly invite your comment. First of all, you -- when you say "we should split Bosnia in two parts," to whom or to which groups would those parts go?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the political decisions that I knew of, as a member of the MUP. The agreement was reached between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Tudjman in order to divide Bosnia. That was more of a friendly chat with Kvesic Branko that I had, and he was inquiring about some friends that were imprisoned in a military camp in Krajina somewhere. However, I maintained very good relationships with all leaders of all ethnicities, and I attempted to pull out these four men from a military camp in Krajina. And since I knew that this telephone conversation was taped, we had some five or six telephone lines, we were a little bit cynical and talked about the situation in Bosnia from both Croatian and Serbian perspectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the question was: To whom or to which group would those parts go? You gave a lengthy answer, but it's still unclear. Would that be Serbs and Croats? Since you're referring to agreement -- or at least a -- you're referring to a -- yes, an agreement between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you very much focus on the question and then answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to direct your attention to the same question the Judge was asking. To whom or to which groups would those parts go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness answered that question, Mr. Tieger. I asked him whether these would be the Serbs and the Croats and he said yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, you indicated in the course of your answer just now that at least part of the conversation was about Kvesic's concern and inquiry about some friends who were imprisoned in Manjaca camp in the Krajina. And he sought assistance in obtaining their release from you, and you indicated that you would help him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I told him precisely that once the president of the state returned from London, I would try to arrange this with him, because that was a military camp in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that kind of situation, who would you ask to effect the release of the people in Manjaca camp about whom Kvesic was concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in the transcript, and I always mentioned that Mr. Karadzic, the president of Republika Srpska, would be the one, and I think that at the time he was in some negotiations taking place in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Dr. Karadzic the only person to whom you could go to influence -- well, first of all let me ask you: Was Manjaca camp controlled by the army, to your knowledge, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And that's what I said in the transcript. It was a military camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Dr. Karadzic the only person to whom you could go to effect or influence potential release of these people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in accordance with earlier instructions, I'm going to turn to a portion of one of the earlier interviews, and that is found at page -- page 14 of the interview conducted on October 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you recall that you had an opportunity to hear this particular intercepted telephone conversation when you spoke with representatives of the OTP on October 1st of this year?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't get -- can you please tell me what are you referring to? I don't have any transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, do you recall hearing this particular intercepted telephone conversation before today?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't have this transcript before me. This is my interview, what I got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you have any recollection on hearing this intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With Branko Kvesic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention to page 17 of the transcript, the B/C/S transcript, of the October 1st interview, page 14 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness apparently has a B/C/S transcript of this interview now, but we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any spare copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I say we don't I don't mean we've mislaid our copy; I mean we've never had one until this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that oversight, Your Honour. I thought that had been the case, and I apologise that it had not been -- I will mention, however - sorry, Your Honour - that it's only recently been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, when you received the English version, I take it you noticed that there was no B/C/S version. You asked for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we very -- we understand it's only recently been produced. We have very explicitly asked for it. It's -- that's only the point.
