utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No. So the answer is yes. Then let's see what comes up before the witness answers the question. The Defence will have an opportunity to tell the Court whether they think that not having the B/C/S version available has such consequences that the questions should not be put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, in this portion of the interview, you can see that there's reference to the conclusion of that tape. You're asked whether you recognise any of the participants. And you mention Mr. Kvesic and Mr. Rezo. And then -- and yourself. You confirm that. And then you indicate that: "Yes. We are mainly commenting on the war and Kvesic was kind of wondering about our former colleagues, where are they and what are they doing now and so on. ... Commenting the war and current state and so on, proposals to end the war and to stop the war. Three Croat men who were captured in Krajina, near Manjaca somewhere, so he asked me if I could help somehow to get these people out of there." Let me stop for a moment and say -- and ask if you now recall discussing this particular intercept that was just played in court during the interview of October 1st.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you continue: "So I promised that I would ask my boss, either military boss or civil boss, to see if he can do something about those three people. That's ... these are the main things." And then you were asked: "Thank you. And who would you have asked?" And your answer was: "Karadzic, Mladic, or Krajisnik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it now you'll put a question, Mr. Tieger, and then I'll give an opportunity to the Defence to see whether there's any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that an accurate reflection of your answer on October 1st and was that a truthful answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the witness is nodding already, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tried to give you an opportunity before the question was answered, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour we're not -- so far as Mr. Tieger asking questions is concerned, we're not disadvantaged by not having the B/C/S transcript. It was obviously important that Mr. Krajisnik [Realtime transcript read in error: "Mr. Tieger"] particularly should have it, so he could follow the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But that goes without saying. Sometimes you would need perhaps Mr. Krajisnik to have it read -- in order to be better able to instruct you. But if it's no problem, let's proceed. But that goes without saying, I think I said; that goes not without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Also, Your Honour, at line -- page 53, line 21, the transcript has inserted Mr. Tieger instead of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not confuse the counsel for the Prosecution and Mr. Krajisnik please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, if I could return to the earlier part of the conversation for a moment. We had been discussing a portion in the first clip portion that was played during which you were talking to Mr. Kvesic and you said: "I just don't know what to do with the Turks. Fuck it. Pay them 24 salaries and let them go, brother. There should be an airlift established with Turkey and let them go and we should split Bosnia in two parts." If we move on farther down to the next page of the English translation, that's page 9, after you and Mr. Kvesic discuss the Elektroprivreda distribution company, the Viktor Bubanj barracks, then Mr. Kvesic says to you: "All right. That's the right way to do it. They shouldn't create problems." You say, "Everyone joins his/her own people," and Mr. Kvesic says, "Certainly." Can you explain to the Court what was meant by your comments about splitting Bosnia in two parts that there should be an airlift and the Turks should be let go and everyone joining his or her own people.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a while ago, I tried to explain that those were political positions taken by the Croat and the Serbian political leaders respectively. When I say the Serbian leaders, that was mainly subscribed to by the Serbian leader, Slobodan Milosevic and other leaders. On the Croatian side, that attitude was rather recognisable on the part of Tudjman, Mate Boban, and other Croatian leaders. As for 24 salaries and an airlift to Turkey, these were just jokes and jests addressed on account of Muslims because we knew that they had to by the Serbian leader, Slobodan Milosevic and other leaders. On the Croatian side, that attitude was rather recognisable on the part of Tudjman, Mate Boban, and other Croatian leaders. As for 24 salaries and an airlift to Turkey, these were just jokes and jests addressed on account of Muslims because we knew that they had been listening to our conversations because they derogatorily referred to us to highlanders and forest people and people who had intercourses with animals and things like that. So this was a kind of propaganda war and we wanted to pay back to those people who listen today our conversations, even play them on TV and who used derogatory terms when speaking about us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that your comments about paying salaries and organising an airlift were not meant to be taken literally. Let me ask you, however, if those were a reflection of the general view, as you -- as it is expressed on page 9 of the English translation, that everyone should join his or her own people.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the territories, that was a political position to open all roads and corridors, and the portions of the peoples who had lived under the control, both militarily and police-wise, by another people, should be allowed to leave and go to the territories where their own people had control. That was the crux of my statement. For instance, if the Croats of Sarajevo left en masse in Sarajevo because they didn't want to stay in the Muslim-controlled territories or where Serbs were the majority. So the Croats demanded either to go to Croatia or to the eastern Herzegovina, and that was my intention for them to open the roads and let them go. Since I think that about 16 or 17 per cent were Croats in Sarajevo, people didn't want to stay there, they left the town, either to join their families or acquaintances and friends either in Croatia or in Herzegovina. You know, Mr. Prosecutor, as far as I knew, there was practice in Sarajevo to ban exit for certain categories of people, whether it be children or women or others and to prevent their movement so that Alija Izetbegovic could simulate that he had a multi-ethnic state or multi-religious, as he used to call it. And all three peoples were fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to a portion of the conversation which was played in the second clip. That's found at -- it begins at the bottom of page 10 of the English translation and continues on to page 11. That's after you mention that Munja was broadcasting everything that you talk about. Do you see that part of the conversation. Mr. Kvesic says, "I can see how smart you are. You wrote it in Latin script and on the other side you wrote it in Cyrillic script." You then said, "We don't want to have a single nation state, man. We want to have a democratic state where the Serbian people would be in the majority". Mr. Kvesic says, "Yes." And you say, "So Croats and Muslims would also have rights. Excuse me, Croats, and the rest of the Muslims after we clean them out." What did you mean by that, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Munir Alibabic is a colleague of mine from the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina who used [as interpreted] for the State Security Service at wire-tapping devices. All these conversations that we are listening to now were recorded by him, and as far as I know, he used to play them, but he used to also twist them, edit them. That was part of the propaganda war. I responded to Kvesic by being cynical and by trying to belittle him and accuse him of twisting things. So in that context, I said that in certain territories where Muslims were in the majority who were otherwise a majority in Bosnia, but that I was never against having a multi-ethnic state, and what I believed, that's what I said, that people should live where they want to live. And that was in the context of relations between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in an earlier response the political positions of Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic, and then mentioned Mr. Boban in connection with that. Were talks or negotiations organised between Serbs and Croats about the possibility of dividing Bosnia between those two ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, before the war and during the war -- there were negotiations before the war, but I don't know about during the war. There were negotiations between Radovan Karadzic and Mate Boban, but what they discussed and in what manner, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know who organised those talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these talks took place either in Mostar or in Konjic before the war, and I think that Branko Kvesic was the one who was the main organiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know which members of the leadership were involved, leadership, either the Croatian leadership or the Bosnian Serb leadership involved in organising those negotiations or talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I cannot remember. I don't even think that I knew about that, because that was either in early 1991 or beginning of 1992. Therefore, I cannot remember who specifically was behind this. You know, Mr. Prosecutor, in Bosnia, everybody talked to everyone, and everyone fought everyone. So everyone was against everyone. I can give you an example. In Sarajevo, where I lived, the Croats and the Serbs did not fight. Kiseljak and -- did not -- Stup did not fight the Serb-controlled locations. But there was a fierce fighting in Herzegovina, Mostar, Capljina, in the valley of Neretva, between the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to turn the witness's -- or direct the witness's attention once again to a portion of the transcript of the October 1st interview. This is found at page 9, lines -- I have it at page 9, lines 33 through 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We don't have line numbering, Your Honour. That won't matter too much as long the pages coincide. If we can be given the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 9 of your version and everyone else's should begin with the words "Deutschmarks."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm talking about a portion that's the last -- essentially the last two questions and answers on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, if I could direct your attention to page 11 of the transcript before you in B/C/S, and that would be the third paragraph from the top of that page. You state: "Mate Boban and it says unintelligible in the English had talks, negotiations at that time, but on political level. But we knew that they were going on so ... They were talking about dividing Bosnia, about dividing Bosnia between Serbs and Croats, but there was nothing," unintelligible word, "stage who is dividing Bosnia," another unintelligible word or words, "so dividing Bosnia in Serbian and Croatian part. The talks between the Serbs and Croats organised by Tudjman and Mate Boban on one side and Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Milosevic on the other side." Mr. Mandic, is that an accurate reflection of your -- of what you said in the interview of October 1st and was that a truthful statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- could I just say, we understand it seems to be a problem throughout some of these documents that items which are described as unintelligible in the English transcript are not indicated in that way in the B/C/S transcript. So we have the words actually there on occasions in the B/C/S transcript and those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- the English are unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite Ms. Cmeric to read the specific part, just put to the witness starting with Mate Boban and so that if you read slowly, that the interpreters could translate that so we catch up the missing words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just to understand the process. I think our transcribers have listened to it in both languages, the English translation and the B/C/S, so it doesn't necessarily reflect the fact that the same -- the person listening should have heard what the other person heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But at least if we have two sources, English and B/C/S, let's try to get as complete a picture as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honour, should -- I should add, the problem exists the other way around as well. Whatever the process, the result is that each way around, sometimes something is marked as unintelligible in one language where in the transcript of the other language it's there in black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any need to fill in the gaps we could do it in the way as we do it. If the gap is in the B/C/S version we could read the English and then fill in the B/C/S. If the gap is in the English, then we could read the B/C/S version. Please, Ms. Cmeric, I'm not a master of your activities, but if you'd be -- please be so kind to read the part just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour. [Interpretation]"Momcilo Mandic: Well, there were at the time negotiations between political leaders. It was that one there Mate Boban, Radovan, and, well, those were ... And we were (unintelligible). We knew of those negotiations about the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, probably between Croatia, between Croatia and between the Croats and the Serbs. That is to say, between Croatia and Serbia from Bosnia and Herzegovina. How shall I put it? (He talks to someone else while the interpreter interprets what he has just said.) Into a Serbian and a Croatian part, between the Serbs and the Croats. There. Which was discussed on the one hand by Mate Boban and Franjo Tudjman and, on the other, by Radovan, Momo, Slobodan, and suchlike."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seem to be quite some differences in the translation. Perhaps, Mr. Tieger, it should be verified in a bit more detail. Because if you're discussing something, that's not the same as organising something, for example. And I noticed such differences and that's not the only one. Let's proceed on the basis of the double source we have now, but perhaps more attention should be paid to the translation of -- or at least the two versions of the interviews. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- I should make it clear. This is a general problem. Ms. Cmeric has done a certain amount of work on this particular document and has drawn attention to sample difficulties a day or so ago to the Prosecution. It isn't really just a question of when we come to a specific point; then, of course, we can deal with this in this specific way, though the results, as Your Honour implied a moment ago, the results do produce something really quite different here. But it's a general problem throughout this particular transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This interview is not in evidence. You're just now putting portions to it [sic] to the witness. The parties are invited to see whether the differences in the two versions are such that it would need further attention in this courtroom. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn next, then, to an intercepted telephone conversation between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Mucibabic on May 26th of 1992. That's ERN ET 0324-9798. That will be in Sanction. I'm just going to play a portion of that, Your Honour. And then we'll ask questions generally from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P462 and P462A for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we start, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not a clip. We're just going to start at the beginning and then I'll ask for it to be halted at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then start.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Unidentified female: Yes? Milanko MUCIBABIC: Hello. Unidentified female: Yes? Milanko MUCIBABIC: Hello. Unidentified female: Yes? Milanko MUCIBABIC: Good afternoon. Unidentified female: Good afternoon. Milanko MUCIBABIC: Is Momo there? Unidentified female: Is this you, Neretva? Milanko MUCIBABIC: Yes, it is. Unidentified female: He's here. One moment, please. Milanko MUCIBABIC: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, hello. Milanko MUCIBABIC: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Yes. Milanko MUCIBABIC: Hello. Momcilo MANDIC: Hello. Yes, can I help you? Milanko MUCIBABIC: I wanted to speak to Momo. Momcilo MANDIC: Hey, Milanko Mucibabic, where the fuck have you been? Milanko MUCIBABIC: Hi there, you fucking minister. Momcilo MANDIC: Where have you been you manager, you manager from Ilijas? Milanko MUCIBABIC: Damn it, old man! Momcilo MANDIC: You're no longer from Sarajevo, right? You're from fucking Ilijas now, right? Milanko MUCIBABIC: Huh. Momcilo MANDIC: You're from Ilijas now, not from Sarajevo. Milanko MUCIBABIC: Old man, it seems I am -- are changing. Momcilo MANDIC: [laughing]. Milanko MUCIBABIC: I up, I down. Momcilo MANDIC: Do you know what they call Sarajevo now? Milanko MUCIBABIC: What? Momcilo MANDIC: Pod Pale. Milanko MUCIBABIC: Fuck off. Momcilo MANDIC: [laughing]. Milanko MUCIBABIC: Well, my man, how are you? Momcilo MANDIC: Well, I'm fucking all right. Milanko MUCIBABIC: You're alive and well? Momcilo MANDIC: I am. What's new in Ilijas? How are things? Milanko MUCIBABIC: Well, it's tense. The whole fucking time, old pal. We responded once and we had 11 dead but they say that there were 80 people dead in Visoko. They had a multiple rocket launcher and we fired about 40 shells on them. And now, old pal, since that army has left from around Zenica they have been grouping, god-damn it. It seems that the people are coming here. Momcilo MANDIC: The Turks from Zenica, right? Milanko MUCIBABIC: I-- Here's a fucking report. They checked the buses in Breza. About eight buses and some trucks arrived. We've made a calculation based on the buses and it seems that about a thousand people have arrived in Breza. Do you know what that means? Momcilo MANDIC: Yes, I do. Milanko MUCIBABIC: It's a problem. We have the artillery but, my god, they've spawned a lot of infantry. Momcilo MANDIC: Yeah. Well, they have fucking nowhere to go. What can they do? And they're hungry. Milanko MUCIBABIC: Old pal. That's where the breaking point will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, again this is not the first time you've had an opportunity to listen to this telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Mucibabic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mucibabic was -- is my long-time friend who was the manager of the sawmill in Ilijas. That was actually a wood processing factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: His ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And where was he during the time this -- what did you understand him to be during the time this telephone conversation was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Ilijas. Prior to that, he used to live in Sarajevo. At the beginning of the war, he -- actually the moment the war broke out, he was working and he was away from Sarajevo and unable to return there. That's why I joked at his expense that he was now a citizen of Ilijas and not of Sarajevo any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to certain parts of the conversation. First, on page 3 of the English transcript, just shortly after -- I think the portion of the transcript we heard ended roughly where you say: "Yeah. Well, they have fucking nowhere to go, what can they do? And ... they're hungry."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUCIBABIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Old pal, that's where the breaking point will be. And ... this ... if this starts ... it stinks in the streets like ... like, like, like ... what's the name ... under." And you say, "Yes, yes." He asks you, "Tell me, how are you? Seselj told me that" - Seso - "told me that you wanted to come and I was in Vogosca, but you didn't ... and so..." And you say, "Well, Krajisnik called me up there so I ... Slobodan Avlijas but I will come one of these days, I must. I'll fly over this week." What did that portion of the conversation refer to, Mr. Mandic? Who wanted you to come, and for what purpose? And why were you unable to do so?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were long-time friends and we merely had to meet to see each other, and nothing more. In this particular conversation, his father had been sick and he had taken him over to Pale to undergo a surgery. And since we did not meet over there at Pale, I promised to come to Ilijas, which is some 40 to 50 kilometres away from Sarajevo -- taking a roundabout road, maybe even more -- and having been long-time friends we merely had this chat; nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger has this part been played to the witness because it -- in the English translation it stops after "Old pal, that's where the breaking point will be." So what follows then is at least not translated by -- but if the parties have no problem to extend this portion of the transcript to a few lines lower then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tried to indicate that the portion to which I'd been directing Mr. Mandic's attention occurred, as I understood it, after that portion that was played in court. And I'm -- and I also indicated I intended to ask Mr. Mandic questions about portions that would not be played because this has -- he has had an opportunity to hear the entire transcript before. If there's a problem with that, we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think we have a problem with that. We're just puzzled as to what the policy is behind the selection of what gets played and what doesn't get played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps the parties could discuss that at another time. But of course we now have a situation where you're referring to those parts not played.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I have no problem playing it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No since the Defence has no problem, I just wondered what happened. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you indicate to Mr. Mucibabic that, as I understand it from the transcript, that you were unable to visit him, that you wanted to come but couldn't, and you explained, well, Krajisnik called me up there, so -- Do you recall for what purpose Mr. Krajisnik called you, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Slobodan Avlijas's name here. He was an assistant of mine and later to become the chairman of the State Commission that toured the camps and detention facilities in Republika Srpska, and it must be an issue that was related to him, since I mentioned Slobodan Avlijas's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say Krajisnik called me up there, where would that be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up at Pale, where the seat of the Assembly was. And Mr. Krajisnik was based there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to a portion of the conversation that takes place somewhat later on. It's found at page 8 of the English transcript and that will be found approximately at the middle of the page. Mr. Mandic, that takes place after, as you're looking through the transcript, there is a discussion, a fairly long discussion, about someone named Babic. You'll see the names on the page Babic, Kalinic, Guzva, Kezunovic. If you pass that, there's a quick reference to Buljakov Potok. There's a reference to Kuso and an incident with him. Going past that. And there's mention of your listening to the radio and hearing something about Mladic and yourself and General Boskovic. Then the portion of the transcript I'm referring to takes place on the page in English after that, a short discussion about Slobodan Avlijas. And then you say to Mr. Mucibabic: "Well, we're only waiting for Lisbon, old man, and for these military school students to finish the whole thing. No, there will surely be a war. War is an option. No other way out."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUCIBABIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Yes. It's the war option now." And you say: "First of all, we should settle the Sarajevo problem through war and then sit down to talk." How was the Sarajevo problem to be settled through war? What was the objective of the war option in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the war objective or the war option with Sarajevo was. Probably to divide Sarajevo along the Miljacka River, the left bank would be the Serbian one and the right bank Muslim. At least that's how I understand it. And we mentioned Lisbon here, that is, the Cutileiro plan, where an agreement was reached by all the three peoples from Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning cantons and the division of Bosnia along ethnic lines, and -- on the basis of cantons, therefore, where there would be ethnic police and the army, depending on the majority people in a particular area. Later on, Izetbegovic gave up this Cutileiro plan, the plan that was forged by mediator Cutileiro and ambassador of Portugal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you understand the ethnic division of Sarajevo to be the objective of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood -- well, this is an off-the-record conversation between oldtime friends. We basically presented our views here rather than the views of the political leadership. Of course, having heard the views of my political leadership, I presented also my views. General Boskovic is mentioned here because the school of the recruits that was within the Marsal Tito barracks was encircled. It's quite known a story that later on 32 young recruits on their way out of the barracks were killed when they were in a column. This was the 6 November Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you express to Mr. Mucibabic during this conversation the attitude of Serb leaders toward Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Milanko Mucibabic was a civilian, a manager of a sawmill. We were long-time friends, talking about our -- exchange our personal views and the atmosphere. We mentioned at least a dozen people who were our common friends, judo sportsmen, Brane, Kusic, Marko -- Babic is actually Dr. Babic, a medical doctor, a urologist, who performed operation at the clinical centre at Pale. He operated on Mucibabic's father. He had a prostate operation. These were our private conversations between people who had known themselves for 30 years. He explained to me, and this was a fact at the time, that Ilijas was encircled. As far as the Sarajevo region is concerned, it was in this area that most people killed [as interpreted] and the fiercest fighting took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, would you please concentrate on the question. In your previous answer you said that you -- that this was an off-the-record conversation between old-time friends and that you basically presented your views rather than the views of the political leadership. The question was whether, perhaps in any other portion, that you presented the -- that you expressed during this conversation, so that might have been at other moments, the attitude of Serb leaders towards Sarajevo and you're telling us a whole story, but not the answer to the question. So the question is: Did you express to Mr. Mucibabic somewhere the position of the leadership in relation to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me direct your attention once again to a portion of the interview between you and representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor on October 1st of this year. And in particular, I'd like to direct your attention to page 23 of the English transcript, page 29 of the B/C/S transcript, in which you're discussing this telephone conversation. And you said: "Phone call was between me and Milanko Mucibabic. He was in Ilijas and I was either in Novo Sarajevo, Kula, or Kasindol." And then you talk for a while about your time together in judo and some of your common friends. And then you say: "And I told Milenko the -- what was the attitude of Serb leaders toward Sarajevo and barracks and everything else." And the you continue to exchange experiences and agree to meet in Pale in two days since it's "long from our place for both of us." Is that an accurate reflection of the statement you made on October 1st of this year, Mr. Mandic, and was that a truthful statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at the time on May 26th, you were the minister of justice of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe I asked you earlier if you understood the ethnic division of Sarajevo to be one of the political objectives of the Serbian leadership. I'm not sure you answered that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so then when you said to Mr. Mucibabic: "We should settle the Sarajevo problem through war and then sit down to talk," was that a reflection of the attitude of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to some comments at page 10 of the English transcript. That's a couple pages beyond the portion we've just looked at. It's after you talk about an event in Hadzici and Vojkovici. And then you mentioned the name Malko Koroman. And then you say: "And how they won't -- tomorrow in Ilijas and Ilidza, my man. Ah, no mercy there, old man. No relations. No way." And Mr. Mucibabic says: "Just expel all and goodbye." And you say: "Expel all and that without weapons and please don't come back any more. Here are your things, your freedom. Here's everything. Just go there and drive." And Mucibabic says: "Run. Where will you go. Go to Visoko, run." You say, "Go to Visoko and ..." Mr. Mucibabic says, "Visoko is not ours. Go to Breza for fuck's sake go there." And you say, "And our people are to be moved in and the buildings and positions filled and so." You had referred earlier to settling the Sarajevo problem through war. Was that the way in which the Sarajevo problem was to be settled through war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 12.30. I'm not finished with this particular intercept, but I'm at the Court's disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can probably spend about two minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could finish in two minutes. That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Moving on in the conversation, Mr. Mandic, again there's a short conversation -- you keep talking -- there's mention of the -- see the word "vidovic" on letter -- page -- a couple mentions of him, and then we get to another portion of the transcript after you indicate that the court is in operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Tieger is losing us here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I need -- my apologies. I'm directing Mr. Mandic's attention to a portion of the transcript found at page 13 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, sometimes without indicating, you're moving from the interview to the transcript of the telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct. And thank you, Your Honour. This -- I am referring everyone's attention at this moment to the telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you did in your last question, whereas the previous to that was about the interview. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Mucibabic says: "And tell me: Will the town be divided? How?" And you say, "It surely will, old man. They -- I don't know, we're waiting for them to come from Lisbon. The alternative is an old one. We defeat Sarajevo and we expel them all the way to Visoko." And Mr. Mucibabic says, "No doubt about it, the town will be ours." And you say: "No doubt about it, old man. Nothing." And again, Mr. Mandic, was that also a reflection of the way in which the Sarajevo problem was intended to be settled through war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation was -- how shall I put it to you, Mr. Prosecutor, to explain to you? An unofficial one. It reflects the war euphoria of the start of the war. I don't think that Mr. Mucibabic and I set ourselves the tasks of solving these issues concerning Sarajevo and the surrounding area. We expressed our views concerning the whole context, the Lisbon talks, and the situation in Sarajevo. This was simply a conversation of mine with a manager of a sawmill from Ilijas who did not make part of any structure at the time, be it civilian or military, belonging to the Serbian people in Ilijas or elsewhere. I think this was a rather informal conversation, not a serious one, merely a chit-chat between two old friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I think everybody here I think understands that you weren't making policy with Mr. Mucibabic in this conversation. But my question is, and I'll ask a different question now: Was your indication to Mr. Mucibabic that "we're waiting for the outcome of Lisbon" and "the alternative to that is the defeat of Sarajevo" a reflection of the attitude of the political leadership toward the situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was your expression that "the defeat of Sarajevo and then we expel them all the way to Visoko" a reflection of the attitude of the political leadership at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time the political view of the Serbian leadership was to divide Sarajevo. The left part of Sarajevo would go to the Serbian entity and the right part would remain in the hands of the Muslims. And I think that the division line ran along the Miljacka River. We did exaggerate in our conversation putting forth some ambitions of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And would the Serbian part of Sarajevo, as well as other parts of Republika Srpska, be inhabited by Serbs and the Muslim part be inhabited by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serbian part, the majority people would be the Serb people, and in the Muslim part, the majority people would be the Muslim people. That was how it was both under the Lisbon plan and the views contained therein and under our own views.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say your own, you mean your own personally and of the Bosnian Serb political leadership; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That question ought to be asked in a less leading form.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say your own, do you mean -- who do you mean? Yourself alone or do you also mean the Bosnian Serb political leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The question was asked in the same way over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this makes no sense. Was this your own opinion or was this an opinion shared by others, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a generally accepted view of the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've overstayed my time, Your Honour, so I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. I would first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness and Mr. Tomic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I asked you yesterday how much you would still need and you said you were confident that until the first break you would finish the examination-in-chief and I know that you had some complaints about interventions, but this really could not explain the extra time you took today since, first of all, there were far less interventions, apart from the one five-minutes-or-less problem. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I apologise for my bad estimate of yesterday. I have one more intercept and I believe another document, and perhaps a few questions. So I would be -- I mean, I'm confident we'll finish in the next session, but I don't know if it's of any value for me to estimate the amount of time it takes to get through a fairly long intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Try to do it as efficiently as possible, and, well, you're confident the Chamber is expecting you to finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- today. We'll adjourn until 1.00. So then you have 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness and Mr. Tomic be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Mandic. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before I move to the next intercept, I just wanted to clarify one point from yesterday's testimony. You explained to us yesterday that you informed Mr. Krajisnik about the poor functioning of the judiciary and that it was making it more difficult to deal with the problems of exchanges of prisoners and conditions in camps. And I asked you then whether you informed Mr. Krajisnik about conditions in camps, and -- that is, I asked you: "Did you tell Mr. Krajisnik what you had heard or were made aware of concerning irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps?" And you said: "In general, I mostly informed Mr. Krajisnik of all the issues that I was aware of, to consult with him on this particular branch of government." I just wanted to ask you whether informing Mr. Krajisnik -- informing Mr. Krajisnik of all the issues included the issues of conditions in detention facilities and camps.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said last time, and that is that whatever I considered or whatever I noticed regarding the government, I informed Mr. Krajisnik and asked him what to do and what should be done to overcome these problems. I most certainly informed him on the situation in Kula, because that was the only facility where I had access to in April and May of 1992. And as for the other facilities, prisons, collection centres, and other facilities where POWs were sheltered or people who had undergone ethnic cleansing and who were held by the army and the police, a commission was set up to visit those camps. They submitted written reports to me and to the government on the situation there, and then through government, we would inform the Assembly and Mr. Krajisnik and all the deputies and thereafter we would propose measures to be undertaken in order to rectify the situation. On behalf of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, Dr. Biljana Plavsic was in charge of this particular segment and she was involved in coordinating the issues with the International Red Cross and other international organisations in charge of these particular issues, including all the commissions from the State Commission downwards to the municipal commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was the information, therefore, available to the government and available to you, as minister of justice, during that time concerning camps and allegations about conditions in camps made known to the president of the Assembly, to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning all the information that I had pertaining to these particular issues, besides government, I also informed Mr. Krajisnik, and he knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me move next to the last intercepted telephone conversation. That's a conversation of May 5th, 1992, between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Kvesic. Your Honour, this is already in evidence as P67, tab 31. There are two indications, also P292, KID 31272 which suggests to me that we need to check and see if it's been duplicated. Let's not do it a third time, if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you recall having an opportunity to listen to this telephone conversation during your interview with representatives of the Prosecutor recently, that is, in October of this year?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to one part of that conversation, if I may. First of all, let me ask you this question, before I do that: As a general matter, were you and Mr. Kvesic talking about what was happening in the war and, in particular, were you talking about whether or not the Bosnian Serbs or the Bosnian Croats were having success in obtaining territories?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I praised the Serbs, how successful they were in war, and Branko Kvesic praised the Croats. He called me Vojvoda and I called Sirva [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I should ask you in connection with that: What was his ethnicity? I think I asked you that before.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat, a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to page 8 of the English transcript, and that's after the initial page of greetings, talk about the families, trying to direct you through there, Mr. Mandic. His question about Mico, discussion about actions in Sarajevo, including Grbavica, Ilidza, Dobrinja, and Nedzarici. Let me ask you, before I pass on that, a portion of page 4, that portion I've just talked about. You say to him: "We came down and cleaned Grbavica." He says, "Is that so." You say, "There, we hold Ilidza, Dobrinja, and Nedzarici all the way to student campus" and so on. Were you relating to Mr. Kvesic the status of Bosnian Serb progress in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could continue on in the conversation. The top of page 8 of the English transcript. At this point you're talking to Mr. Stojic. Can you tell us quickly who he was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stojic was a colleague of mine from the time when we worked at the SUP and he was assistant minister for finance and common affairs. He was a Croat and a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at that portion of the conversation, Mr. Stojic asks you: "Please. Tell me. I have heard that they are fucking pushing, you know." And you say: "But of course. They pushed us all the way to Skenderija." He says: "To Skenderija," and there's laughter. You say: "They pushed all the way to Skenderija." He says: "Listen is there any way to resolve this peacefully." You say, "What?" Mr. Stojic says: "Well, this in Sarajevo." And you say: "Only when they give up everything from Skenderija and around there, then we will accept and leave for them everything from the eternal flame and all the way up." Mr. Stojic says: "But they are left with nothing then." And your answer is: "Fuck them. They didn't want to do it nicely through negotiations. Well, now they'll get nothing." Now, when you refer to being pushed all the way to Skenderija and there's laughter, what are you conveying to Mr. Stojic in that part of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a little bit of ridiculing the Muslim propaganda. On their TV channels and in their newspapers they claimed that they had reached Lukavica, took over Dobrinja, reached as far as Jahorina, took over Ilijas and Vogosca. And knowing that this conversation was listened in by Munir Alibabic, I said that we had been pushed all the way to Skenderija, which is the centre of the town. So it was a little bit of a ridicule on my part. There was a row between former colleagues Jusuf Pusina and Munir Alibabic and myself, because I knew they were listening on my conversation and I wanted to ridicule them, because they spoke of me on the TV and in the newspaper, saying that my mother had cursed me not to wage war and that she was begging me, crying not to proceed. And that is what they did on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And later in that same portion of the conversation, when you say: "They didn't want to do it nicely through negotiations. Well, now they'll get nothing," is that a reference to the failed negotiations that preceded the outbreak of the war, the Cutileiro negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were held either in March or April of that year. And I even think that even after that the negotiations continued between the Muslims and the Serbs, that is, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and Mr. Krajisnik, in Lukavica and in the Assembly in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Although I can't find the specific reference, Mr. Mandic, I believe there's a reference in here to -- during this conversation to your moving on from MUP to Justice. And this conversation occurs on May 5th. I know you told us that you were formally appointed to ministry -- as minister of justice on May 19th. Do you recall when you first knew you were going to be minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Probably at page 13, isn't it, top of page 13 of the English, starting at the very bottom of the previous page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that was in early May or late April. I cannot remember exactly. I heard the news from the then-minister of MUP, Mico Stanisic, who informed me that the political and state leaderships had decided that I should take over the Ministry of Justice and to start building the Serbian Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in the interests of time, I'm going to move on past this exhibit and ask you a couple of questions. What, insofar as you know, was the relationship between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know either of them, but I had information that they were good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know whether they -- okay. Let me ask you: What was their relationship during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the relationship was excellent at the beginning of the war. Then it was rather correct. And it seems to me that toward the end there was some mistrust and disagreement in pursuing policies, particularly in personnel policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you say "toward the end," what period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is when I was the director of the bureau in Belgrade. During those two years and after that. I frequently communicated with Mr. Krajisnik, and even went to Pale from Belgrade, and I mainly was privy to this relationship that I don't think were quite excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke earlier about your position as the director or chief of the bureau in Belgrade. Would the nature of that position be such that it could be considered a kind of promotion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the bureau of the government of Republika Srpska, and all ministries had their representatives in this bureau, appointed by the responsible ministers. Myself, my deputy, and a few other men were coordinators there. The minister of defence, the Ministry of MUP, the Ministry for the Wounded and the Veterans, worked with Serbia, cooperating in providing shelters for them, including every other aspect of cooperation between Belgrade and Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krajisnik instrumental in you getting the position with the bureau in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I was dismissed on the 16th of November. The first prime minister, Mr. Djeric, resigned, and I was left jobless then. There was a conflict between me and Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, and also Radovan Karadzic, because I had a reputation of an urban Serb who was tolerant and unwilling to concede to certain aspects of governance. At the insistence of Biljana Plavsic, I left for Belgrade because our relations were very bad ever since 1991. Thanks to Momcilo Krajisnik, I was given this post in Belgrade; otherwise, I would have been out of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Krajisnik instrumental in your obtaining the position you did with the bank?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you one last exhibit, Mr. Mandic. I'd like that marked next in order. It's a document entitled "Saint Michael's patron saint's day."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand it's a bit of a nuance, but may be important nuance in translation that -- I'm informed by Ms. Cmeric that -- that what the witness will have heard, of course, in his own language, which was then translated "Was Mr. Krajisnik instrumental in your obtaining a position you did with the bank," that the translation here, of course I'm reliant on Ms. Cmeric, is more in the sense of "involved". So and instrumental does carry a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- significance in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please try to seek verification, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P463.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll first clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, to what extent was Mr. Krajisnik responsible for your obtaining the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I really don't know why then on that basis Mr. Tieger doesn't just picked up "involved" as the foundation for the question and then put that point to the witness in those terms rather than pick a third term.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, to what extent was Mr. Krajisnik involved in your obtaining the position with the bank?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is not receiving translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher -- You did not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear the interpretation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Mandic on the right channel?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The witness said he doesn't have a written translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's first, before we move to the next document, the question put to you by Mr. Tieger was: To what extent Mr. Krajisnik was involved in your obtaining your position with the bank. Could you please first answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the largest possible extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was he therefore responsible for your obtaining that position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He found this job for me and arranged for me to get it. Had it not been for Mr. Krajisnik, I would not have become the manager of the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And now if I could turn your attention to that document, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that's the upper left portion in the B/C/S version, that is what appears in our translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this appears --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we make one -- before we get into the question, just one observation. We think it's obviously a mistake, but in the middle paragraph during the commemoration, the third name there, there's Milenko after Tomo Kovac, there's Milenko and it's Milenko somebody else altogether, we believe. Karisik is what we suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milenko Karisik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's Karisik rather than Krajisnik. Yes, please proceed. I think we can correct this middle portion, second line, third name, Milenko Karisik rather than Krajisnik. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does this document, Mr. Mandic, reflect a celebration that was held on 21 November, during which the MUP of Republika Srpska celebrated its Patron Saint's Day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the 21st of November. It was the Patron Saint's Day of the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at that occasion, were awards presented to persons who had -- were people honoured for their involvement with and contribution to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And let me clarify this to you, Mr. Prosecutor. The Nemanjic's Order is awarded by Mr. Karadzic, as president of the Republic, to the then-minister of MUP, then the deputy minister of -- that is, to Mico Stanisic, as the minister of MUP, Momcilo Mandic as deputy. Tomo Kovac, I don't know if he was chief of the security station at Ilidza. Milenko Karisik as the commander of the special unit of MUP, and to the MUP as an institution, as a ministry. The Order of the Karadjordjevic's Star was given to seven members of the ministry. I don't know who. And MUP of Republika Srpska, headed by the Minister Mico Stanisic, presented their -- the Golden Badges as credits to the president of the Republic, Radovan Karadzic, to the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, the Ministry of the MUP of Serbia, Zoran Sokolovic, to Mico Stanisic, to Jovica Stanisic. I think this man was the chief of the state security of the MUP of Serbia. To Milan Martic from the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. He was the MUP minister. To Mihalj Kertes, who was the chief of the customs in Serbia, to Radovan Stojcic, deputy minister of the MUP of Serbia, to Momcilo Mandic, myself, as a former member of MUP, and to the general, Ratko Mladic, as the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were all these individuals presented the Golden Badge of the ministry for their contributions to the common effort pursued by those people and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe there was anyone present here from Serbia, not even the person from Krajina. What's his name? Milan Martic. I don't think that Ratko Mladic was at this ceremony either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But was the award bestowed on them, either personally or in absentia, because of their contributions to the common effort?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to this other award, that was presented by the minister of the MUP of Republika Srpska, whereas the other awards were given to some five or six people from Sarajevo. That was the awarding of the Nemanjic Order that was presented to these people by the president of the Republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, may I ask you again to concentrate on the question. The question was whether this Golden Badge was awarded to the persons mentioned for their contribution to the activities of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can ask it this way, Your Honour, if it makes it easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why did they get the award, insofar as you know, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a decision taken by Mico Stanisic in relation to people who were either from the MUP of Serbia or from the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is why. You now told us who gave it and where those who received it came from, but the question is simply: Why did they get this award?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not take part in the presenting of this badge. I was merely invited as a party receiving this. I don't know what credit was referred to here by presenting these awards, nor whose idea it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you must have had an idea -- well, perhaps you, for the Nemanjic Order, but what in your perception was the reason why they got the order, the Golden Badge of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that I received it as a former assistant minister and deputy minister, and these people probably took part in reinforcing, strengthening the structure of the MUP. If you have in mind these people from Serbia, outsiders, helping with the equipment, with the weaponry, in order to strengthen the institution of the Ministry of the Interior, I believe that this is the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a structure or just in whatever way they contributed to the work or the existence of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't think the word "structure" was there in the original answer. We don't know where it's come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course I -- when you said in your previous answer that these people probably took part in reinforcing, strengthening, and then of the MUP, what did they reinforce or strengthen? The MUP or anything specific of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The MUP itself, most certainly, because I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's -- perhaps forget about "structure."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the Prosecution's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I think that there's -- it doesn't make that much sense at this moment to offer an opportunity to Defence to start to cross-examine the witness. So, therefore, that will be delayed until tomorrow. You did send a message to the Senior Legal Officer, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- if tomorrow morning I would give you an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, what could we expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That I would decline the opportunity, Your Honour, and so that -- because the message was a courtesy to indicate to the Trial Chamber in advance, I probably in just two sentences should say in open court that the -- it indicated that -- well, it's drawn to my attention, Your Honour, that perhaps the witness should be asked to leave before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we have not finished yet your examination, so we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning. I instruct you as I did the previous days not to talk with anyone about the testimony you have given or still are about to give. Then you're excused until tomorrow morning, same courtroom, 9.00. Mr. Tomic, you're excused as well. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Stewart. Well, the message was clear, and I think it's good to that you refer to it in open court. You know that the ruling of the Chamber was that you would be given an opportunity to cross-examine the witness and on specific issues, that is, especially if you would need, as it was said then, further cross-examination on -- related to lately disclosed documents, you could apply for that, which -- and I hope that there was no uncertainty about that, that the Chamber expected you to -- if you wanted to use your right to cross-examine the witness, which is a right, on any other subject, that you would do it once the examination-in-chief had been concluded. I also understood from your message of yesterday that you may apply at a later stage for the cross-examination as a whole, so not just on the lately disclosed documents. Of course, we haven't seen any such submissions, but you will have to look at them if such submissions or if such applications are made. But I take it that it was clear to you -- well, whatever your thoughts about it might have been that the Chamber expected you to cross-examine on all the -- well, let's say timely or at least earlier disclosed documents and on any other subject right after the conclusion of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. Your Honour does -- I just had mentioned the message, but Your Honour's remarks over the last couple of minutes certainly do, as one would expect, of course, accurately reflect the message, Your Honour. But I do confirm that the Defence team, and I -- I believe I can speak for the whole team, the Defence team, we believe we understand the Trial Chamber's ruling the other day in response to our application at that time to defer Mr. Mandic's cross-examination generally. We understand the Trial Chamber's expectation that we would proceed on -- in the areas that you have mentioned in relation to Mr. Mandic's cross-examination. We believe our understanding of that is clear. And our conveyed message as a courtesy in advance to the Trial Chamber is now our position that we -- I said we may. Your Honour, Chamber the expectation certainly is that we will at some appropriate point make an application to bring Mr. Mandic back for an entire cross-examination. We will, of course, then, have to support that application with all the material which we believe appropriate to put before the Court at that stage to support that application, both in effect retrospectively to cover the position as it is now and the position as it will be -- which is the key point -- at the point we make the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think tomorrow morning we'll -- the Chamber will start to give you the opportunity and we would not be surprised if you decline at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. That won't come as a total surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I bring to your attention is the following: That -- the Chamber fully understands for what reasons you're declining, because you -- the Defence takes the position that they have not had sufficient time and facilities to prepare the cross-examination. That's clear to the Chamber. At the same time, I draw your attention to the fact that if the Chamber allots time for preparation, a week off, at a certain moment as we did consistently now and we are still about to do, I expect a further Scheduling Order before the recess. And it has already been, well, presented to you in a kind of a draft form and we had already some oral argument on that. But if the Chamber finally gives a scheduling order and if it does so after it has heard the parties in some detail, as we did last time, then of course the -- such an order could not be circumvened by asking in respect of every witness. And of course you didn't ask for every witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I haven't, Your Honour. I clearly haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, that you didn't ask that for crime base witnesses. But if with some frequency the Defence applies for delay of the cross-examination, then it might well disturb the scheduling as ordered by the Chamber. And I'm not saying that under no circumstances the Defence could apply further delay of cross-examination in respect of a witness; but at the same time, I'm drawing your attention to the fact that if that happens and if that happens frequently, then that would finally disturb the whole scheduling by the Chamber, a scheduling which is based upon an assessment of what would be sufficient, adequate time for the preparation of cross-examination of a witness, I would say adequate time and facilities for the preparation of cross-examination of the witness. I'm just telling you this, that you should keep that in your mind. We will --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply say straight away, Your Honour. All those matters, thank you, Your Honour, and I'm sure it's helpful to all concerned and especially to Mr. Krajisnik to understand that, because I do my best to explain the position to him from time to time as well. But all those elements that Your Honour outlines are well understood by counsel for the Defence. And, well, every relevant factor is a matter to be taken into account on every application at the time every application is made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Make things perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will now distribute the English version of the Kljuc [phoen] diary, which we're still waiting for. Yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would like to thank again the interpreters and the technicians for again a couple of more minutes that we've stolen from them. It's highly appreciated that you show such flexibility where we are not able to finish on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of December, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
